lesson.title: The Perfect 36: How the Nineteenth Amendment Became Law
lesson.summary: The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in August 1920, barred the federal government and the states from denying the right to vote on account of sex, ending decades of organized struggle by American women.
lesson.body:
By the early twentieth century, American women had been organizing for the vote for more than seventy years, and the reform energy of the Progressive Era gave that campaign new momentum and new tactics. Progressive reformers already believed that expanding the electorate and cleaning up politics could fix the problems of industrial society, and suffragists argued that women voters would bring exactly that kind of moral seriousness to government. The amendment's text is simple and direct: the right of citizens to vote "shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex." Getting those words into the Constitution, however, took a coordinated national campaign that combined patient lobbying with public pressure.

Congress passed the amendment on June 4, 1919, sending it to the states for ratification. Suffrage leaders then had to secure approval from thirty-six of the forty-eight states, a process that meant fighting state-by-state battles all over again even after winning in Washington. Momentum built through 1919 and into 1920, but by the summer of 1920 the count stood at thirty-five states, one short of the total needed, and opposition in the remaining Southern states was fierce. Everything came down to Tennessee, where the state legislature was closely divided. On August 18, 1920, a young state representative named Harry Burn changed his vote to yes after his mother wrote urging him to support ratification, and Tennessee became the "Perfect 36," the deciding state. The Nineteenth Amendment was certified on August 26, 1920.

The amendment's passage was the culmination of the long struggle traced through the broader women's rights movement, sharpened by the specific strategies and organizations of the women's suffrage movement and by leaders like Susan B. Anthony, who did not live to see this victory but whose legal and organizational work shaped the campaign that won it. Even so, the amendment's promise was not fully realized for all women at once. Many Black women, especially in the South, continued to face poll taxes, literacy tests, and outright intimidation that blocked them from voting for decades afterward, a reminder that constitutional text and lived access to the ballot are not always the same thing.
